question: In June 2023, TikTok users began posting parody horror clips after sampling a limited-edition purple beverage sold by a major fast-food chain. These clips showed teens acting deranged or pretending to collapse, with the purple liquid smeared messily around their mouths. The berry-flavored drink was named for and colored after a rotund mascot whose exact species has never been clarified by the company. It was released as part of a birthday meal celebrating that mascot's debut, which dates back to 1971. McDonald's had no hand in starting the parody trend, but embraced the free publicity it generated. For 10 points, name this viral berry milkshake tied to a purple McDonald's mascot's birthday, which spawned a wave of mock-death TikTok videos in 2023.

In October 2023, a glycine manufacturer based in Shijiazhuang, a city in Hebei province, began posting sincere-sounding promotional videos that TikTok users embraced ironically, spawning a devoted fan following. A parody clip using an AI-cloned voice to imitate the company's ad style went viral in March 2024, cementing the joke. The humor also targets customers who order gray-market bodybuilding compounds like BPC-157 or TB-500 from small overseas manufacturers, joking about entering a "Joker arc" after a promised week-long delivery stretches to two weeks. These compounds are short chains of amino acids, not full proteins, and are popular among biohackers despite little regulatory oversight. Companies like Shijiazhuang Donghua Jinlong became unlikely internet celebrities through this trend. For 10 points, give this two-word slang term combining a nationality with a term for these short amino acid chains, used to describe an online meme fandom around imported research chemicals.

A 2015 academic paper examined 4chan greentext stories narrated by users under this label, arguing they created a feminine space within the site's overwhelmingly male community. The archetypal story in this genre follows a 24-year-old woman recounting an embarrassing dating mishap, often illustrated with a reaction image nicknamed "possiblebf.jpg". This term combines the label 4chan posters adopt instead of a username with a prefix marking the poster's gender. Know Your Meme catalogs the "24-year-old" variant of this label as one of its most-referenced greentext archetypes. Such stories typically begin with the phrase "be me," followed by an age and this term, before recounting a humiliating romantic failure. For 10 points, give this 4chan slang term for a female anonymous poster.

In 2015, tabloids reported that actress Charlize Theron had ended her relationship with actor Sean Penn using this method, without any prior conversation or warning. The term describes abruptly and completely cutting off all communication with someone, especially a romantic partner, with no explanation given. Some credit journalist Rachel Thompson with coining this term's modern dating sense, while others point to a 2014 comedic web video. This word likens someone's sudden disappearance from a relationship to vanishing into thin air, as though they had become intangible. Dating apps and social media are often blamed for making this behavior more common in the 2010s and 2020s. For 10 points, name this dating slang term for abruptly cutting off all contact with someone without explanation.

This crudely drawn, MS Paint-style bald cartoon face was first shared to the German imageboard Krautchan in 2010 by a user of the same name. One of its most common variants, created by 4chan posters in late 2017 while mocking a Nintendo Switch enthusiast, is drawn with an open, toothy grin and blank eyes; it takes its name from the plant milk also used to make tofu. A dedicated imageboard devoted to producing that toothy-grinned variant was founded in September 2020 by users banned from 4chan's now-defunct question-and-answer board. The original bald-faced version is best known for a viral comic in which the character cries at his computer, captioned "I wish I was at home". This face family serves as a blank canvas for online reaction images representing everything from despair to smugness. For 10 points, give the shared name for this family of simply drawn cartoon reaction faces, whose grinning variant is nicknamed for a plant-based milk.

In January 2020, Twitter user @anyonesromance posted an image of a blushing emoji captioned with this adverb, sparking widespread use among K-pop fan accounts wanting to express interest in an idol without seeming creepy. Meme historians trace an earlier, more mocking use of the word to parody posts by self-proclaimed male feminists who awkwardly over-asserted their support for women. Paired with the word "looking," this adverb became a popular caption for images expressing restrained admiration toward an attractive subject. It functions online as a tongue-in-cheek qualifier appended to a statement of attraction, signaling that the poster appreciates what they see without crossing a line. The word's ironic use spread from Twitter fandom culture into a broader shorthand for acknowledging desire while maintaining propriety. For 10 points, name this adverb, often paired with "looking," used sarcastically online to add a veneer of manners to an otherwise thirsty statement.

This two-word internet insult tells its target to step away from a screen and go outside instead of continuing to argue online. It is frequently directed at people passionately debating niche topics like anime ship wars or video game lore, mocking them as "chronically online." The phrase began appearing on Twitter as early as 2015 but exploded in popularity between 2019 and 2021. It implies that making physical contact with a lawn would serve as proof that the target has actually left their house. The insult assumes the recipient spends so much time indoors online that reconnecting with nature has become a foreign concept. For 10 points, give this internet insult telling someone to step outside and make physical contact with a lawn.

Houston rapper Sauce Walka helped popularize this slang term for an impressively stylish look on his 2014 mixtape "Saucemania", later defining it in a Genius interview as meaning "to be a king" or "to be a winner". A viral December 2020 render depicted three video-game crewmates from Among Us wearing Nike Jordans, nicknamed for having an abundance of this quality. A widely shared TikTok video showed a teenager defending a new outfit from a disapproving stepmother, coining a catchphrase that demanded she respect this slang term for the outfit's style. Synonymous with "swag," this slang term likens having a standout personal look to liquid falling in small amounts. It traces to mid-1990s and early 2000s hip-hop culture before gaining renewed popularity through 2010s and 2020s internet memes. For 10 points, give this slang term for fashionable style or swagger, whose name evokes a liquid falling drop by drop.

On February 28, 2016, Black Twitter user @_PettyCrocker helped popularize a hashtag mocking women who boasted about being ideal romantic partners while shaming single women for their clothing or dating choices. TikToker Hannah Montoya's skits, starting in March 2021, popularized comedy sketches mocking a type of woman who denigrates other women in order to seem more appealing to men. The label for this archetype implies she desperately wants to be chosen over other women, sometimes at the expense of her own dignity or her peers' reputations. A 2023 CNN explainer described this term as being applied to women accused of putting down other women to win male approval. Critics have debated whether the label unfairly polices women's individual choices and personalities. For 10 points, give this hyphenated two-word slang term, often followed by "girl," describing a woman who seeks male validation by criticizing other women.

High schooler Gabby Rasson coined this slang term in 2013 to describe people who were slightly off-trend, though it stayed mostly obscure for years. On March 30, 2021, copywriter Hallie Cain posted a TikTok explaining that certain hat slogans, a specific hair-care brand, and captions quoting pop star lyrics all fit this label, sending it viral. The American Dialect Society voted this term its informal word of the year for 2021. It describes millennial-associated aesthetics or fashion choices perceived as outdated or overly try-hard, and is pronounced "chew-gee". Debate over the term sparked wider conversations about generational taste and whether it was simply a new way to judge women's style choices. For 10 points, name this slang term for something already out of fashion, often applied to millennial trends like skinny jeans or side-swept hair.

Composer Mikhail Chertishchev wrote this song for his daughter, performer Betsy, wanting to depict "an incredibly cool guy that everyone likes, but where the girls should be even cooler". Co-writer Mukka researched teenage internet slang to pen its chorus, which repeats an internet term for a stoic, unbothered, alpha-adjacent male archetype. Released October 3, 2024, by Betsy alongside singer Masha Yankovskaya, this Russian EDM-pop track went viral on TikTok in late November 2024, spawning countless "brainrot" remixes and dance videos. Its title takes that slang term, borrowed from a Greek letter, repeats it, and then adds the English word for a young male. Political commentators in several countries later criticized the song and its associated dance trend as an inescapable presence among children. For 10 points, name this viral 2024 song and TikTok brainrot meme whose title doubles an internet slang term for a stoic male archetype before adding "boy".
